analysis.one_liner: Makes public utilities return excess deferred tax money to their ratepayers instead of keeping it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got past the House Ways and Means Committee: it was referred there in February 1989, hearings were held in October 1989, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When Congress cut corporate tax rates in 1986, electric and gas utilities had already collected money from their customers to pay taxes at the old, higher rates. Under the 1986 law's 'normalization' rules, utilities were allowed to spread the benefit of that difference to customers over many years instead of refunding it right away. This bill would repeal those rules, so that the extra money utilities collected would flow back to ratepayers through lower bills or refunds. The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of regulated electric and gas utilities. If the bill had passed, the excess deferred tax reserves — money customers paid toward taxes that turned out to be lower after the 1986 rate cut — would have been returned to them through their rates rather than kept by the utility companies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the section of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 that extended normalization requirements to utilities' excess deferred tax reserves, which is the mechanism that lets utilities hold the benefit of the corporate rate reduction rather than pass it to customers [S2] [S3].

The bill's own title states its purpose is to remove the provision 'which limits the benefits to consumers from the effect of the corporate rate reduction on deferred tax reserves of public utilities' [S3].

The repeal would take effect as if the provision had never been enacted, restoring the pre-1986 treatment under which excess deferred taxes were not protected by normalization and could be returned to ratepayers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public utility companies, which would have to give up accumulated excess deferred tax reserves and return them to customers through lower rates or refunds, reducing the funds the utilities can hold on their books.

drawbacks.text: Utilities argue normalization rules let them recover costs gradually and finance new power plants, and that returning deferred taxes abruptly would disrupt utility financing and could pressure future rates — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh [S2] [S3].

The refunds would go only to customers of regulated public utilities in proportion to their bills, so the benefit is uneven and reaches customers over time through rates rather than as a direct payment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a straightforward transfer: money collected from customers for taxes at pre-1986 rates goes back to those customers instead of staying with the utilities. The utilities' financing argument is real — deferred tax reserves are a low-cost funding source for plant investment — but the pre-1986 rules Congress chose in 1986 had permitted the money to flow back to ratepayers, so the bill restores a previously accepted arrangement rather than creating a novel one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the tax-writing committee, which held a hearing on it but never reported it out, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Dorgan of North Dakota introduced the bill on February 28, 1989, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1] [S5].
Twelve members cosponsored the bill: eleven House Democrats and one House Republican [S4].
The Ways and Means Committee held hearings on the bill on October 4, 1989, but the committee never reported the bill to the full House, and no vote ever occurred [S5].
The bill expired at the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991, without reaching the House floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public utility companies kept the excess deferred tax reserves that the bill would have directed back to ratepayers. No one was worse off on paper, but customers never received the refunds the bill was written to deliver.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public utilities, which kept the money

for.name: Rep. Byron L. Dorgan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Utility Ratepayer Refund Act of 1989 to repeal the normalization provision and return excess deferred taxes to utility customers

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill in February 1989 and held a hearing in October 1989, but never reported it to the House floor; the bill died there when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was mostly but not entirely partisan: 11 of the 12 cosponsors were Democrats and one was a Republican, and the House's Democratic majority controlled the committee that held the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities to return excess deferred tax reserves — money collected from customers for taxes at pre-1986 rates — to ratepayers. Utilities' interest in keeping those reserves runs directly against customers' interest in lower bills, which is precisely what the bill was written to change [S2] [S3].
